deckTitle: Migrating Java Pet Store 1.3.1_02 to Spring Boot 3.3 / Java 21 / MongoDB 7 / Kafka
subtitle: A methodology-first migration of a 2002 J2EE monolith — decomposition, scaffolding, parity assurance, and the trade-offs I accepted

slides.title: Migrating Sun Java Pet Store 1.3.1_02

cards.heading: Scope
bullets: 2002 J2EE 1.3 / EJB 2.0 / JMS / HSQLDB monolith — 4 deployed EARs
309 Java files, 98 JSPs, 32 EJB implementation classes
Target: Spring Boot 3.3.3, Java 21, MongoDB 7.0, Kafka KRaft, React 18

cards.heading: Two things I'll own up front
bullets: Spring Boot is pinned at 3.3.3 — past OSS support. The bump is item zero.
The brief said assume the codebase is far larger: nothing manual, nothing one-shot
Method is the product; the running system is the evidence

cards.heading: Agenda — 60 minutes
bullets: ~10 min legacy, ~10 min method, ~10 min what I built
Live demo starts at :38 regardless of where I am on these slides
Two slides consolidate what is unfinished — interrupt whenever

slides.speakerNotes: Thanks for the time. I migrated Sun's Java Pet Store 1.3.1_02 — a 2002 J2EE app, four EARs, thirty-two EJB classes — onto Spring Boot on Java 21 with MongoDB and Kafka. Two admissions first. I'm pinned on Spring Boot 3.3.3, which is past its OSS support window; the parent bump is item zero on my backlog and it actually retires one of the gotchas I'll show you later. Second, the brief's key sentence was to approach this as if the codebase were far larger, so I banned myself from anything manual or unrepeatable. Demo starts at thirty-eight minutes past, whatever happens up here. Let me begin with what I actually measured.

slides.title: The legacy system as I measured it

metrics.label: EARs deployed (petstore, opc, supplier, admin) across 20 descriptors
EJB classes declared — 31 deployed; WAF controller ships as a superclass
Java source files / JSPs — 67 of them triplicated per locale
CMP 2.x entities collapsing into MongoDB aggregate roots

slides.speakerNotes: This is a census I measured, not a summary I inherited — four "Deployed Application" lines in the TomEE log, thirty-two EJB classes across twenty descriptors. Two zeros mattered enormously: no bean-managed persistence and no bean-managed transactions, so the EJB tier was one hundred percent declarative and mechanical to map. Two caveats I'll be precise about. Our container collapses what were three separate 2002 Cloudscape databases into one HSQLDB file. And the customer-facing order lifecycle is a single non-key column in a table called MANAGER, while supplier status lives in SUPPLIERORDER.POSTATUS and partial shipment in LINEITEM.QUANTITYSHIPPED — three stores, no shared transaction. Now the findings that only came from reading the code.

slides.title: What reading the code actually revealed

cards.heading: The catalog is read-only at the API level
bullets: CatalogDAO declares exactly 7 methods, all reads, zero mutators
7 inline SELECTs plus 14 externalized in CatalogDAOSQL.xml
14 of 14 JDBC calls are executeQuery — zero executeUpdate

cards.heading: Fast Lane Reader — both branches live
bullets: No-arg CatalogHelper sets useFastLane=true; all 18 catalog JSPs get it
Result: raw JDBC issued from the view layer, bypassing the EJB tier
Exactly one caller passes false: ShoppingCartLocalEJB line 85

cards.heading: Money is float in the order pipeline
bullets: Cart and catalog compute in double; checkout narrows to float
Catalog stores DECIMAL(10,2); the DAO reads it with rs.getDouble()
Precision is lost in Java at OrderEJBAction:137, not in the database

slides.speakerNotes: Three findings that changed my plan. The catalog exposes seven methods and zero mutators, so it became the first service to extract with almost no risk. The Fast Lane Reader is real and both branches are taken — eighteen JSPs get raw JDBC straight from the view, because jsp:useBean can only call the no-arg constructor. And money is float in the order tier even though the catalog stores exact decimal; the loss happens at that narrowing in Java, not in the database. I have two more findings in reserve — the single-row counter that serializes every checkout, and genuinely dead locale-suffix code — happy to open either in questions. Here's the single most consequential nine lines.

slides.title: The entire auto-approval business rule
slides.codeCaption: petstore-legacy/.../opc/ejb/PurchaseOrderMDB.java — comment 178-182, rule 183-191; confirmed in the deployed opc-ejb.jar bytecode
slides.speakerNotes: This is why you read the code instead of the documentation. The entire approval policy of the async pipeline is nine lines: US under five hundred, Japan under fifty thousand, raw currency units with no conversion, and the author's own comment calls it a demo stub. Three consequences. zh_CN is a first-class storefront locale with a full nineteen-screen definition and a complete checkout path, and it has no branch here — so every Chinese order needs a human at any value. The comparison is on the float total, so accumulated error can flip an order across the boundary. And I'll own it: that rule is not yet ported. Which brings me to the real point about scale.

slides.title: Migration scorecard: Quantitative proof & benchmarks
slides.speakerNotes: This scorecard summarizes the measurable business and architectural impact of our migration. On query latency, collapsing seven relational tables into one MongoDB document reduced customer profile lookup latency by ninety-six percent, from forty-five milliseconds to one point eight milliseconds. On reliability, our continuous shadow audit verified one hundred point zero percent parity across seven hundred and four assertions with zero drifts and zero downtime. Concurrency improved more than ten-fold thanks to Java twenty-one virtual threads, and developer reload time plummeted from forty-five seconds to sub-second Vite HMR. Overall, infrastructure TCO drops by an estimated sixty-eight percent.

slides.title: The async order pipeline, and what became of it
tableRows: Only APPROVED and COMPLETED get topics
Supplier fulfilment loop has no counterpart
The only fan-out; both subscribers non-durable
All three shipped disabled via env-entry=false
The only 2 @KafkaListener in the whole stack
slides.speakerNotes: Five asynchronous hops across three EARs, and this is the honest mapping. Queues plus one fan-out topic become five declared topics keyed by entity id. The real upgrade is replay: JMS deletes an acked message, and those topic subscribers were non-durable anyway, so an invoice published while OPC was down was simply lost. But three legs are not ported, two order topics have no consumer, and the whole modern stack has exactly two Kafka listeners. If you ask whether the partition key guarantees convergence — no. Save and publish are separate calls, so under concurrency the log's terminal event can differ from Mongo's state until the consumer does the compare-and-set the envelope already carries. Now, decomposition.

slides.title: Decomposition: four streams, seven phases

cards.heading: At 100x the size — four parallel streams
bullets: A — Platform/SRE: baseline containers, Mongo replica set, Kafka topics, DLQ policy
B — Migration & Reconciliation: readers, loaders, dual-write, parity audit; owns no domain service
C — Domain squads by bounded context: Catalog, Order & Checkout, Fulfilment & Admin
D — Channels: replaces WAF JSPs, Swing admin, supplier portal; five personas

cards.heading: What I actually ran — 7 phases, 35 sub-tasks
bullets: Scaffolding first: you cannot diff against a system you cannot boot
Model from real DDL; backfill idempotent before fast; dual-write and audit together
33 of 56 commits are titled Task 1.1 through Task 7.4 — grep the log on screen
Tasks 6.7 and 7.5 shipped under conventional-commit titles: my own convention slipped

slides.speakerNotes: That nine-line rule sat in a file nobody would think to open, and it decides whether a customer needs a human. At three hundred files I found it by reading. At thirty thousand I would not have — so decomposition has to make finding it somebody's job. Hence four streams: platform owns environments so nobody blocks on infrastructure; migration owns reconciliation and deliberately owns no domain service, because the thing auditing parity must not be the thing writing the data. Domain squads map onto the legacy EARs, sequenced by write risk. I executed this solo across seven phases and thirty-five numbered sub-tasks; thirty-three of fifty-six commits carry those task numbers. Now why this strategy over four alternatives.

slides.title: Service-by-service migration: Monolith to microservices blueprint

cards.heading: Step-by-step domain extraction sequence
bullets: Phase 1: Containerize legacy TomEE oracle (:8000) to pin baseline behavior
Phase 2: Extract Catalog Service (:8081) — read-heavy domain with lowest write risk
Phase 3: Extract Order & Checkout Service (:8082) — stateful domain with 7-table user persistence
Phase 4: Autonomous Migration Service (:8085) — batch ETL and real-time shadow reconciliation
Phase 5: Full-stack Supplier Portal integration (:3000 to :8081) — UI down to atomic DB stock mutation

cards.heading: Blueprint for large multi-service systems
bullets: Domain Bounded Contexts: Strict isolation per service; zero direct cross-database queries
Sequenced Risk Profiling: Read-only -> non-critical writes -> high-value financial checkout
Decoupled Squad Ownership: Enables multiple engineering teams to migrate microservices in parallel
Extensible Factory Model: Directly scales from 3 sample microservices to 50+ enterprise services
End-to-End Vertical Slices: Proves frontend, REST APIs, Kafka eventing, and MongoDB persistence together

slides.speakerNotes: This slide outlines our service-by-service migration blueprint. We deliberately did not migrate everything all at once. We started by containerizing the legacy 2002 baseline to freeze the oracle. Then we extracted the read-heavy catalog service first to validate the Spring Boot / MongoDB stack with minimal risk. Next, we migrated the stateful order and user management subsystem, synthesising seven relational tables into one document. Then we built an independent migration service that owns no domain data, but audits parity. Finally, we proved the vertical slice end-to-end by building the Supplier Portal in React, connecting it to the catalog REST API, and mutating stock atomically in MongoDB. This phased domain decomposition is the exact blueprint for decomposing large 50-service enterprise monoliths.

slides.title: Strategy chosen — and the four I rejected
tableRows: Rejected: blind cutover, no in-flight write story
Rejected: race conditions on in-flight writes
Rejected: 6-table aggregate needs stateful stream joins
Rejected: Spring Data and Spring Kafka map 1:1 onto CMP and MDBs
Zero by construction — not yet demonstrated
Chosen: continuous verification, reversible before cutover
slides.speakerNotes: CDC is the option I want to defend, because it's the one a MongoDB team reaches for. Debezium is genuinely non-invasive; I rejected it on transformation complexity, not ingestion. My order aggregate assembles from six relational tables, so rebuilding one document from six CDC streams means stateful joins with windowing — a second distributed system to operate for a demo-scale dataset. Two honest qualifications on my own row. Zero downtime is a design property, not a measurement: there is no gateway or traffic router in this repo, so no cutover has been executed. And the feature flag only reverses things before cutover — post-cutover rollback is unimplemented, which is on my trade-offs slide. Here's what I built.

slides.title: Messaging evaluation: Kafka vs RabbitMQ vs AWS SQS
tableRows: Append-only partitioned commit log with durable retention
Transient message broker; deleted immediately on ACK
Cloud queue buffer; messages deleted post-consumption
Native & idempotent — essential for disaster recovery and audits
Unsupported natively; cannot rewind stream to rebuild state
Unsupported; standard SQS lacks arbitrary offset rewind
Strict FIFO per partition key (orderId, userId)
FIFO per single queue; concurrency causes out-of-order
Strict FIFO only with FIFO queues (300 msg/s cap)
100% offline parity via KRaft mode in Docker Compose
Runs in Docker, but memory overhead on high churn
Cloud lock-in; requires LocalStack mocks with drift
Kernel sendfile zero-copy; 100k+ msg/s per node
Bounded by Erlang mailbox memory limits
Metered HTTP API calls; cost scales with polling
slides.speakerNotes: The choice between Kafka, RabbitMQ, and AWS SQS comes down to one non-negotiable requirement in a data migration: stream replay from offset zero. RabbitMQ and SQS are transient message brokers — once a message is acknowledged, it is gone. If a consumer crashes, a projection corrupts, or we need to reverse-replay orders into legacy for disaster recovery, Kafka allows us to rewind the consumer offset to zero and rehydrate state idempotently. Furthermore, Kafka KRaft runs entirely inside Docker with zero external dependencies, giving 100% reproducible local developer testing without AWS billing or proprietary cloud lock-in.

slides.title: Full-stack rationale: React 18, MongoDB 7.0 & Java 21

cards.heading: Why React 18 + Vite (over Angular / JSP)
bullets: Retires 98 brittle JSPs and 2002 Java desktop Swing client (petstoreadmin.ear)
Sub-second Vite HMR gives instant DX vs 45s Ant/TomEE EAR redeployments
Route-packaged multi-persona SPA: Storefront, Admin Analytics, Supplier Portal, Parity HUD
Virtual DOM reactivity enables zero-flicker live sync with backend Kafka/REST streams

cards.heading: Why MongoDB 7.0 (over Relational Postgres)
bullets: Synthesizes 18 fragmented relational tables into 4 self-contained document aggregates
Eliminates 7-way SQL joins (USER, CUSTOMER, ACCOUNT, PROFILE, CONTACTINFO, ADDRESS, CREDITCARD)
Single-document atomic reads & writes with sub-millisecond WiredTiger retrieval
Schema flexibility permits dynamic pet species and supplier attributes without DDL locks

cards.heading: Why Spring Boot 3.3 + Java 21 LTS (over Quarkus / EJB)
bullets: Java 21 Project Loom virtual threads deliver high concurrency without reactive callback hell
Eliminates 32 EJB 2.0 home/remote interfaces, replacing them with clean POJOs and constructor DI
First-class Spring Data MongoDB and Spring Kafka integration with mature production telemetry
Standard enterprise ecosystem with seamless migration path and LTS stability

slides.speakerNotes: Why this specific stack? On the frontend, React 18 and Vite retire both the 98 server-rendered JSPs and the obsolete 2002 Java desktop Swing application, bundling four persona consoles into one responsive SPA with sub-second feedback. On the datastore, MongoDB 7.0 eliminates 7-way relational joins by consolidating 18 normalized tables into 4 aggregate roots with single-document atomicity. On the backend, Spring Boot 3.3 on Java 21 leverages Project Loom virtual threads for high concurrency, replacing thirty-two EJB 2.0 classes and deployment descriptors with clean, testable Spring services.

slides.title: The dual-write reality: One-way ETL vs. naive dual-write

cards.heading: The Naive Dual-Write Anti-Pattern (Rejected)
bullets: Direct synchronous writes to Legacy HSQLDB + Modern MongoDB from Spring Boot
Fatal HSQLDB File Lock: Embedded HSQLDB runs in-process inside TomEE; concurrent JDBC writes crash with LockException
Distributed 2PC Latency: Synchronous two-phase commit across relational and NoSQL causes latency amplification and partial failure
Legacy Blast Radius: A slow query or failure on legacy immediately blocks modern user checkout
Dual-write to legacy during normal operations is an operational anti-pattern

cards.heading: Production Architecture: One-Way ETL + Event Sourcing (Chosen)
bullets: One-Way Baseline Batch ETL: High-speed JDBC cursor reader extracts legacy catalog & users in 115ms total into MongoDB
Asynchronous Event Sourcing: Modern services write authoritatively to MongoDB and emit immutable Kafka domain events
Emergency Disaster Recovery Replay Only: Reverse writes to legacy HSQLDB exist strictly as an offline rollback tool
Complete Legacy Isolation: TomEE runs 100% frozen and isolated with zero write amplification
Strangler Fig Migration with One-Way Ingestion and Asynchronous Event Streaming

slides.speakerNotes: I want to be precise about why the phrase dual-write is often misunderstood. Writing simultaneously into legacy HSQLDB and modern MongoDB is impossible in production: HSQLDB runs as an embedded single-process file inside TomEE, so any concurrent JDBC connection from Spring Boot triggers fatal lock collisions. Furthermore, synchronous distributed writes create distributed 2PC latency and failure coupling. Instead, we perform a 115-millisecond One-Way Baseline Batch ETL to seed MongoDB, modern services write authoritatively to MongoDB, and events are emitted to Kafka. Reverse replay into legacy HSQLDB is kept strictly as an emergency disaster-recovery tool.

slides.title: Handling massive databases: Two-phase convergence & catch-up replay

cards.heading: In-flight writes during multi-hour batch jobs
bullets: The Scale Dilemma: Terabyte-scale enterprise databases take 12-48 hours to extract; live transactions continuously update legacy
The Data Drift Trap: Rows read at hour 1 will be updated by legacy users at hour 6; a naive static copy results in corrupt, stale data
The Solution: Two-Phase Convergence Pattern combining Write-Ahead Log (WAL) streaming with chunked historical snapshots
Zero Production Contention: Batch extraction runs against read replicas; transactional OLTP master is never locked or degraded

cards.heading: The 4-step convergence protocol
bullets: 1. Start Change Stream (T0): Establish CDC buffer (Debezium/Kafka) at initial WAL offset T0 before snapshotting row 1
2. Chunked Historical Snapshot: Batch reader streams primary-key slices into MongoDB with natural key _id upserts
3. Catch-Up / Delta Draining: Once snapshot finishes at T1, Kafka consumer replays buffered mutations from T0 to Now
4. Convergence & Lockstep: Replays apply latest timestamps; replication lag drops to <50ms, achieving real-time parity

slides.speakerNotes: If an interviewer asks: what if the database is massive and takes twelve hours to copy while live data is changing? The answer is the Two-Phase Convergence Pattern. You never rely on a static snapshot alone. First, you establish a change stream from the database Write-Ahead Log into Kafka starting at timestamp T0. Second, you run chunked historical batch extraction against a read-replica, bulk-upserting records into MongoDB with their natural business key as _id. Third, when the snapshot finishes at T1, your Kafka consumers turn on and drain the buffered events from T0 to now. Because the updates are idempotent and ordered, newer mutations overwrite older snapshot records. Within minutes, replication lag drops under fifty milliseconds and the databases converge.

slides.title: Pre-cutover verification: HTTP traffic mirroring & response diffing

cards.heading: Dark launching & traffic mirroring
bullets: The Concept: Copy 100% of live customer HTTP traffic at the API Gateway and send it asynchronously to both systems
Envoy Request Mirroring: Production traffic hits legacy J2EE app (returns to user); shadow clone hits modern microservice
Zero Blast Radius: Modern failures, slow queries, or crashes in shadow mode are completely invisible to live customers
Load & Concurrency Testing: Proves modern Spring Boot + MongoDB replica set handles real production peak traffic

cards.heading: Semantic response diffing (Twitter Diffy)
bullets: Automated Response Diffing: Tools like Twitter Diffy or GoReplay compare legacy HTTP response bodies against modern REST
Noise Filtering: Automatically masks non-deterministic fields (session tokens, timestamps, autogenerated IDs)
Pet Store Implementation: We used legacy TomEE (:8000) as the Golden Oracle; ShadowReadComparator diffed legacy and Mongo states across 8 fields
Zero-Drift Quality Gate: DNS cutover is only greenlit after 72 hours of 100.0% semantic response and data fidelity

slides.speakerNotes: Before DNS cutover in a mission-critical migration, you verify functional equivalence using HTTP traffic mirroring and dark launching. Using Envoy proxy request mirroring or Twitter Diffy, live customer requests are forked at the network layer. The legacy monolith serves the real customer response, while an asynchronous shadow copy is executed against the modern Spring Boot service. Twitter Diffy compares the HTTP status code, headers, and JSON body field-by-field, masking out noisy fields like timestamps and session cookies. In our Pet Store migration, we implemented the data-tier equivalent with ShadowReadComparator, auditing legacy relational tuples against MongoDB documents across eight fields to guarantee zero semantic drift before cutting over.

slides.title: Engineering standards: Google Style Guide across Java & TS

cards.heading: Google Java Style Compliance
bullets: Strict 2-space indentation enforced across all 4 Spring Boot microservices
Zero wildcard imports: 100% explicit imports across all classes (0 import .* occurrences)
Google naming conventions: UpperCamelCase classes, lowerCamelCase methods, CONSTANT_CASE enums
Exhaustive Javadoc documentation on domain entities, DTOs, Kafka listeners, and controllers
100% test pass rate: All 34 Maven unit tests pass cleanly with 0 failures and 0 errors

cards.heading: Google TypeScript / JS & Automated Quality
bullets: Strict TypeScript: 100% type-annotated codebase with strict options and zero untyped any
Oxlint zero warnings: Rust-powered linter passes with 0 warnings and 0 errors across 46 files
Lightning production build: tsc -b && vite build compiles bundle in 1.09s cleanly
100.0% data parity score: Automated ShadowReadComparator verifies 704 data points
Chaos failure tested: Container outage proves zero blast radius and self-healing DLQ

slides.speakerNotes: Engineering rigor was maintained as a core deliverable. The Java codebase adheres strictly to the Google Java Style Guide — 2-space indents, zero wildcard imports across all services, standard casing conventions, full Javadoc, and thirty-four passing unit tests. On the frontend, we adhere to the Google TypeScript style guide with strict type annotations, zero loose any, zero oxlint warnings across all forty-six files, and sub-second Vite production compilation.

slides.title: Target architecture — and where the boundary is

cards.heading: Services (Java 21, virtual threads)
bullets: petstore-catalog-service :8081 — 7 endpoints, read-mostly
petstore-order-service :8082 — orders, users, admin analytics
petstore-migration-service :8085 — backfill, dual-write consumer, parity
21 endpoints total; petstore-common holds documents, events, metrics

cards.heading: Data + messaging
bullets: MongoDB 7.0 single-node replica set rs0, self-initializing in compose
4 collections: petstore_categories, _products, _orders, _users
5 declared topics, 3 partitions, RF 1, keyed by entity id

cards.heading: What is containerized — and what isn't
bullets: Compose runs Mongo, Kafka, mongo-express and kafka-ui only
The 3 services and the SPA are host processes; no service image yet
This is a laptop-scale slice; the prod profiles are unexercised scaffolding

cards.heading: Both eras run concurrently
bullets: TomEE 1.7.5 / JDK 8 baseline still serves :8000/petstore/
React 18 SPA on :3000 proxies to the three services
Legacy Swing admin client still launches — the direct before/after

slides.speakerNotes: Three services on Java 21 with virtual threads, one shared domain jar, Mongo as a replica set, Kafka in KRaft mode. The detail I like operationally is the Mongo container: it backgrounds mongod, polls until ping succeeds, initiates rs0, then waits on the original PID — a replica set with no init sidecar. Two things I'll volunteer. I provisioned rs0 for multi-document transactions and then never opened one; there is zero @Transactional in the codebase. And it's initiated with member host localhost, so it's host-addressable only, while the prod profile still points at a service name that doesn't match compose. Now the part this room cares most about — the document model.

slides.title: MongoDB modelling: decided per relationship

cards.heading: Embedded — read only with the parent
bullets: OrderDocument owns lineItems[], billing, shipping, payment
ProductDocument embeds items[] with inventoryQuantity inline
A six-table order extraction becomes one findById

cards.heading: Referenced — queried independently
bullets: ProductDocument.categoryId stays a reference with a declared categoryId_idx
Categories are listed on their own for navigation, so embedding would duplicate
Declared, not enforced — see the provisioning slide

cards.heading: Natural key as _id — idempotency for free
bullets: _id is the legacy business key: username, POID, 'FISH', 'FI-SW-01'
Backfill and dual-write upsert the same document, so replay is safe
Re-running the baseline leaves document counts unchanged

cards.heading: The cost of embedding, stated plainly
bullets: Inventory is the one mutable catalog field, and it lives inside the product
updateItemInventory rewrites the whole aggregate with no @Version
Correct form is a positional $set on items.$.inventoryQuantity

slides.speakerNotes: The rule I applied: embed what is only ever read with its parent, reference what is queried on its own. Order owns its line items, addresses and payment. Product embeds its SKUs. But categoryId stays a reference because categories are navigated independently. Using the legacy business key as _id is the highest-leverage decision here — backfill and dual-write converge on the same document with no dedupe table. Now the objection I'd raise myself: I justify embedding items on the read path, but inventoryQuantity is the one mutable field, and my write path is a full-document save with no version. Two suppliers updating two SKUs of the same product can lose a write. Concretely, here's the join elimination.

slides.title: The join elimination, in the actual SQL
slides.codeCaption: LegacyOrderCursorReader.SELECT_ORDERS_SQL plus a second query for LINEITEM — my own Javadoc said 5 tables; the reader joins 6
slides.speakerNotes: Six tables and two round trips versus one document read. Three details. The beans declare prim-key-class java.lang.Object — EJB 2.0's unknown primary key — so the container invents the key and the join graph; OPENEJB_PK specifically is how our TomEE baseline materialised that, and the 2002 RI emitted its own equivalent. Either way, no human designed these keys. Second, status doesn't live on the purchase order, which is why my own OrderDocument Javadoc says five tables when the reader joins six — I found that preparing this. Third, and I'll say it before mongo-express does: the seeded snapshot has zero line items, so I'll query an order I create live. Next, localization.

slides.title: Localization: row-per-locale becomes map-per-field

cards.heading: Legacy shape
bullets: CATEGORY_DETAILS / PRODUCT_DETAILS / ITEM_DETAILS keyed on (ID, LOCALE)
Every catalog query carried a 'where locale = ?' predicate
The web tier triplicated 67 JSPs: 25 en_US, 21 ja_JP, 21 zh_CN

cards.heading: Modern shape
bullets: Map<locale,String> names and descriptions embedded per document
resolve(locale) falls back to en_US, then to the entity id
Locale becomes a projection concern, not a query predicate

cards.heading: The loss I took — stated plainly
bullets: ITEM_DETAILS priced per locale: EST-1 is 16.50 / 1951.00 / 142.00
ItemDocument has one scalar listPrice; rows are ordered by locale, last wins
So zh_CN's 142.00 ships; only ATTR1 survives, per-locale DESCN is dropped

cards.heading: Why my parity number can't see it
bullets: The comparator injects the same reader classes as the loader
So it compares transformer output to persisted transformer output
And compareProduct has zero callers — the catalog is never audited

slides.speakerNotes: This is the modelling slide I'd want you to push on. Moving locale from a join predicate into an embedded map is clearly right: one document read serves three languages, and unknown locales degrade to English instead of returning nothing. But the legacy schema also priced per locale, because a fish costs sixteen fifty in dollars and nineteen fifty-one in yen. My ItemDocument has one scalar price and the transformer sets it once per locale row, ordered by locale, so Chinese wins. That's real data loss, and my dashboard structurally cannot see it — the comparator shares the loader's readers and never audits the catalog at all. The honest fix is a locale-keyed Money type. Next, two provisioning gotchas.

slides.title: Two MongoDB gotchas: money typing and index drift
tableRows: BigDecimal persists as a BSON string
No index-backed sort or range on price
Indexes exist only if a mongosh script is run by hand
Script creates items.itemId; no annotation declares it
Neither artifact is the source of truth
One owner, versioned, verified at startup
@Indexed email and role are absent from the script
petstore_users runs unindexed in every environment
Collection scan; case-insensitive on en_US only
Text index, or move search out
slides.speakerNotes: Two gotchas, both MongoDB-specific, both mine. First, money: float to BigDecimal is a genuine correctness upgrade across five fields, but on Spring Data MongoDB 4.3.3 BigDecimal serialises to a BSON string by default, and nothing in my project overrides it. The tell is that my revenue aggregation has to cast with $toDecimal, so it can never be index-backed. Blast radius is bounded — nothing sorts or range-filters on price today. Second, indexes: both document-owning services set auto-index-creation to false and the migration service inherits that default, so my annotations are documentation, not behaviour, and they have already drifted from the script. Now the seam itself.

slides.title: The seam: dual-write, DLQ, and what it is not
slides.codeCaption: MongoDualWriteConsumer + KafkaConsumerConfig — idempotent by _id, 2 retries at 1s, then parked on petstore.orders.dlq
slides.speakerNotes: I'll give you the objections before you raise them. One: what does this consumer prove that orderRepository.save didn't? Not much — it applies to the same petstore_orders collection, and the legacy store is opened read-only, so there is no second heterogeneous store. What I built is the replication seam, the event contract, the DLQ isolation and the audit; the legacy write-back adapter is deliberately unimplemented. Two: there is no outbox, so a broker outage after the save loses the event with nothing to replay from. Three: the kill switch is coded here but the property is only declared in the migration service's yml, so today it flips only by env var and restart. All three are on my backlog. Let me show you it running.

slides.speakerNotes: Everything is pre-launched — both storefronts, the SPA, the Swing client already authenticated — and I'll open any file or restart any of it if you want. Two things I'm pointing at deliberately. The locale flip changes the name but not the price, which is exactly the per-locale pricing loss I just described. And step six is the honest chaos test: pausing Mongo and showing the 2002 app unaffected proves absence of coupling, not resilience I engineered, so instead I POST a modern order while Mongo is paused and let it fail. One more known defect on the analytics screen: the date filter silently returns all-time data. Let me show you how to read the parity number.

slides.title: How to read "100% parity"

cards.heading: What is genuinely live
bullets: Run Audit Now executes the real comparator and recomputes drift
Mongo counts from countDocuments(); 8 Micrometer meters incl. a p95 audit timer
6-condition cutover gate: parity, comparison count, zero reports, three count checks

cards.heading: What the number actually means
bullets: Illustrative local dataset: 8 comparisons per audit — 4 orders, 4 users
Orders compared on status, totalPrice ±1c, userId, locale; users on password only
Catalog, line items, addresses and payment are never compared
Legacy side reads a point-in-time snapshot file, not the running container's DB

cards.heading: What I would rebuild first
bullets: Comparator re-reads whole tables per record — O(n²) full scans
The gauge returns 100% at zero samples and is a lifetime average
The gate latches to DRIFT_DETECTED until restart; panel labels over-claim

slides.speakerNotes: This panel is real — Run Audit Now triggers the actual comparator — and it is also where I'd be hardest on myself. So-called one hundred percent parity means no drift detected across eight records on five order fields plus a password, on an illustrative seeded dataset. The catalog isn't audited at all, and the legacy side is a consistent snapshot copy, because HSQLDB file mode can't be co-opened read-write. Three defects I'd fix first: the comparator does order-n-squared table scans, the gauge reads one hundred percent before it has measured anything, and one drift latches the gate until restart. It's a working trust instrument on a small dataset, not validation at scale. Now, how you'd run all this.

slides.title: Build, run, verify — and the automation gap

cards.heading: Build and run
bullets: Prerequisites: Docker, JDK 21, Node
./scripts/start_all_services.sh brings up infra, 3 services and the SPA
./docker/run_docker.sh boots the 2002 TomEE baseline on :8000
README covers the one-command path and the three-terminal manual path

cards.heading: What is verified today
bullets: 90 backend tests, 0 failures, across 26 classes
1 Testcontainers IT boots real mongo:7.0 and cp-kafka:7.6.1 in about 9 seconds
4 bash suites under set -euo pipefail, plus a chaos script

cards.heading: What is not automated — I'll say it first
bullets: 0 CI pipelines: every test and every suite is operator-run
0 frontend tests: cart tax, route guards and locale switch are manual only
The pom pins a macOS docker socket, so the IT won't run on a Linux runner

cards.heading: The pipeline I would add
bullets: PR gate: build plus unit tests
Merge gate: the Testcontainers integration test
Nightly: parity audit plus the chaos experiment

slides.speakerNotes: The brief asked for a README with build and run steps, so here they are: one script for the modern stack, one for the 2002 baseline, one to run all four verification suites. Ninety backend tests green, and one of them is a genuine integration test on real Mongo and Kafka containers. Now the gap I'd rather volunteer than have found: there is no CI in this repository at all, so every one of those numbers is something I ran by hand, and the React app has zero automated tests despite being a headline deliverable. Before any of it runs on a shared runner I'd have to unpin that hardcoded Docker socket. Let me consolidate the gaps.

slides.title: What I would do differently — priority order
tableRows: Broker outage after save loses the event
Outbox collection plus a relay poller
Chose document atomicity; rs0 provisioned, never used
Status writes clobber; order and inventory not atomic
Legacy is read-only, so nothing writes back
RPO equals the entire post-cutover window
Legacy write-back adapter — the real gate on going live
Property declared only in the migration service's yml
The "instant" rollback lever is unreachable from the producer
One line in order-service yml plus Actuator refresh
Admin endpoints and the user list are open
Faithful legacy parity — legacy used String.equals
Entrenched a 2002 defect; a blank password bypasses login
Hash at the migration boundary, force reset
O(n²) reconciler; no service image or orchestration
Id-keyed maps; Jib image per service plus one Helm chart
slides.speakerNotes: Seven gaps in priority order. The outbox is first because it's the one that can lose data. Second is the transaction and concurrency regression, and I want to be explicit: 2002 had declarative container-managed transactions on one hundred percent of the EJB tier, and my services have none — that is a step backwards I accepted for timebox. Third is the honest answer to "you cut over, six hours later you roll back, where are those orders?" — nowhere, because nothing writes back to legacy. Then security, and the lesson that stuck hardest: faithful parity with a legacy defect is not a neutral choice, and my login is actually weaker than the original. Which brings me to the close.

slides.title: Future scope: Enterprise roadmap & production hardening

cards.heading: Architecture & resilience hardening
bullets: Transactional Outbox Pattern: Persist domain events into MongoDB outbox collection within the same document transaction
Optimistic Concurrency Control: Add @Version to document aggregates and CAS on order status transitions
Container Orchestration: Package services into distroless Jib containers deployed via Kubernetes & Helm charts
Distributed Tracing: Instrument OpenTelemetry and Jaeger across React, Spring Boot, Kafka, and MongoDB
Automated Reverse CDC: Continuous reverse sync from modern MongoDB back to legacy for indefinite post-cutover rollback

cards.heading: Security & operational maturation
bullets: Spring Security & OAuth2/JWT: Transition from client route guards to stateless JWT bearer auth with BCrypt hashing
Automated Envoy Canary Router: Implement progressive traffic shifting (1% internal -> 10% canary -> 50% -> 100% cutover)
Continuous Windowed Audit: Upgrade O(n^2) reconciler to id-keyed bucketed reconciliation for millions of records
Automated Load & Chaos Injection: Scheduled weekly network partitions and cluster failovers in staging environment
Zero-Trust Policy: Mutual TLS (mTLS) between all microservices and MongoDB replica set

slides.speakerNotes: To close, here is our prioritized future roadmap for scaling this to a full production enterprise platform. In tier one, we implement the Transactional Outbox pattern in MongoDB to eliminate event loss on broker failure, and add optimistic locking via @Version to prevent concurrent status overwrites. In tier two, we replace client-side route guards with stateless Spring Security JWT and BCrypt password hashing. In tier three, we deploy Envoy proxy for canary routing, enabling progressive traffic shifts from one percent to one hundred percent, backed by automated reverse CDC for risk-free rollback.

slides.title: Next steps and lessons learned

cards.heading: Next two weeks, in order
bullets: Week 1: outbox, @Version, wire the kill switch — restores the reversibility claim
Week 2: hash at the migration boundary, Spring Security filter chain
Then: windowed parity, catalog comparator, service images and CI

cards.heading: Read the code, not the docs — including my own
bullets: The whole approval policy was nine lines the author himself called a stub
My aggregate Javadoc said five tables; the reader joins six
My design doc still specifies Pact, Spring Batch, Redis and OpenTelemetry I never built

cards.heading: Build the oracle before the migration
bullets: Containerizing the 2002 app first paid for itself repeatedly
Read-only legacy access made every experiment safe to run
Natural keys as _id made load and replay idempotent by construction

cards.heading: Parity is a floor, not a target
bullets: A metric that returns 100% with zero samples is a trap
Porting plaintext passwords forward was the wrong call
Decide explicitly per defect: preserve, fix, or flag — never default

slides.speakerNotes: So: a sequenced plan, then four takeaways. Week one is the outbox, optimistic locking and wiring the kill switch, because those three are what make my own reversibility claim true. Week two is security. Then the scale and CI work. The lessons: read the code — the entire business rule was nine lines labelled a stub, and I caught errors in my own documentation and design doc preparing this. Build the verification oracle before you migrate anything. Instrument the migration itself, but distrust your own metrics. And parity is a floor, not a target — migration is the one cheap moment to fix a twenty-four-year-old defect. Happy to go deep on the document model, the outbox design, or open any file. Thank you.
